I feel bad writing this review, because even with a thumbs up, I feel like I'll be cutting the game off at the knees. But better you know the truth, I guess.

First off, the game is based on a WC3 custom map called Night of the Dead. You are space marines prancing around a Mars colony full of zombies. You select a suit (read: class), a primary weapon, a secondary weapon, 4 suit components (read: skill...not trees. Paths, maybe? 5 sequential, mostly passive abilities), up to 3 powerups (which add some bonuses at the cost of other penalties), and you go off to try and survive a ~1 hour long match. You find items and accomplish objectives which will strengthen your team, while endless waves of zombies try to murder you to death. The customization isn't that deep, but you'll find plenty to tinker with if you're the fiddy sort. I enjoy it greatly.

Singleplayer exists, but it's not the focus. You control 4 marines and run around doing the same kind of stuff. It's fun. Probably not full price fun, but fun nonetheless.

Multiplayer is the real heart of the game. In order to stand any chance, each player must possess basic tactical acumen and practice it for the entirety of the hour. Further, you have to possess some expertise in your class and use the right abilities at the right times, and understand the flow and structure of the game. Put simply, you are going to lose. You're going to lose a lot. It's a very hard game. Some vets will come and say "oh, no, it's not hard, just git gud". Well, fair enough, but the game has a very steep learning curve. It's simple to play, very difficult to master. That's a good thing, I think. But still, expect to lose a crap ton.

There is a meta-progression, where you increase in rank (which unlocks stuff, and gives some very minor bonuses) and suit rank (gives very minor bonuses to a particular class when you play it), and medals (also small, but welcome bonuses to individual suits). It starts off fast, but becomes extraordinarily grindy to max. But that's OKAY. When I say very minor bonuses, I mean it. The game is much like Left 4 Dead, or Vermintide in that the game is almost entirely about good teamwork, and somewhat about individual skill, and very little about raw stats or xp. About 70% of winning is teamwork, 20% is individual competence, 9% is having enough xp to play the classes you need, and 1% is xp-rewarded stat bonuses. On top of all that, you can prestige (yes, lose one full 0 to max xp amount) in order to get even more tiny bonuses. That said, unless you're a total no-lifer, don't expect to max anything here.

Now let's talk about the community. In order to accomplish anything, you will need to bring friends or make friends. I was able to take my little gaming collective of 3 into the game and we died a bunch, but we were able to improve considerably and also not hate or ruin the game for each other. That's pretty ideal. If you can't bring your own friends, you'll probably need to find a few veterans on the forums. The community is incredibly small, and if you just join a public game, you will get 5 minutes in, and then die, and everyone else will die, and everyone will swear a lot and blame each other. You will swear that nobody else in the world but you knows how to play the game better than a chimpanzee with a congenital learning disability. You will rage that it will take you 9650 games to reach the next rank if you keep dying on wave 2. You will go out into the darkness, and there will be a great wailing and gnashing of teeth. Sometimes, you'll sit in the lobby and there won't be enough people to form one lousy game.

Yeah. You need to either bring your own community to this game, or else ingratiate yourself to the crusty old veterans who've solved this puzzle ages ago.

But overall, I recommend this game as everything about it is a labor of love. They adapted Night of the Dead from Warcraft 3 to bring the game to its fullest potential, to introduce it to new people, many of whom don't even own Warcraft 3. It's certainly not for the money, given the sad state of the community. And the players work on it out of passion too. I see more and higher quality guides for Red Solstice than I see for most AA games these days. The people who make and play this game obviously care about it a lot. There is some talk about how to strengthen the community, but the fact of the matter is, in my opinion, you just can't. It's a niche game, it's a difficult game, it has virtually no marketing, and the story is the narrative version of a toupee. 99% of gamers would take one look at it and turn right around. Red Solstice is a hidden co-op gem, on the same level as AI War. It's a very rare taste. It'll never be very popular, and that's fine, because it doesn't need to be. It's just fun. I like it a lot.

One last note: expect to do a lot of research. Many of the deeper mechanics are buried within documentation that exists only on the forum, or one guy's steam guide, and some haven't been written down at all.

Been playing this for a while now but only casually. Got into it quite early in the Beta, when it was still a bit of a buggy mess. You still played it, because it was fun. The learning curve is nothing to laugh about, and it is not exactly the noobfriendliest of communities, especially some of the first players sometimes lack the nerves to deal with new players. 
Once you get into it though, you will have an awesome experience. Highly tactical, once you get off "Soldier"-difficulty, relies 100% on each teammate. 

By now the game has several different maps, playable on 4 difficulties and a handful of different modes that change up the experience like the "Red Storm" mode where you are weak when outside of buildings, but stronger inside, or swarm and fast modes that increase the pressure on your squad. All with 8 different classes, completely customizable with different weapons and abilities, that have to be utilized harmoniously to win.

Protip: Get a mic. Theres a central TRS teamspeak server, that anyone in the game lobby can give you, and coordinating an 8 man team is just so much easier with voice. Learning the game and getting taught will be 10 times faster if you go on ts with one or two of your squadmates.

The best way to get into it would be to grab a few freinds, put it on easy, and just jump into it. You will die. A LOT. but thats fine, and you will have fun getting to know all the different abilities and weapons before getting on with the pros who might be more interested in winning than teaching.

Sadly, this game has a very small player base, so don't expect to play 8 man games 24/7. There are high times each day, where there are usually 2-4 different games going on, but expect to do some waiting in lobby for members. However, this means that you get to know people very quickly, and if you are somewhat nice and don't harass people, you will be welcomed in the community.

In this game, you control the main character and give orders to a squad of 3 elite Marines with two-digit IQ per squad. It is therefore not surprising that orders must be given several times in a row and constant monitoring must be carried out to ensure that they do not fall into fire, acid, or are blown up by a mine.

Unfortunately, the game is full of bugs that have never been fixed. Some of them can completely break the game, so you have to replay the mission in the hope that you won't encounter them this time, or perform unnecessary actions to overcome them, such as using the combination: tactical mode – camera movement – normal mode; rinse and repeat, while the camera should automatically follow your Marine when you press a certain button. In some story missions this is crucial.

It is quite common to see a message "This skill is missing description / It can damage your squad mates" with an incorrectly displayed cooldown in addition (2 seconds, but in reality, it is 200 seconds) – so you don't even know what this skill is supposed to do and trying to use it can lead to defeat.

Disarming a nuclear weapon doesn't work on the first try, and you may think you have disarmed it, but then it explodes. It is written that you can explode it using detonation, but it doesn't work. Quite often, auto-aim takes on a life of its own, constantly switching between modes. Sentry turrets can mysteriously disappear even if they haven't been destroyed. The nuclear weapon that is supposed to help you get to the extraction point appears at the other end of the map when you are running out of time to evacuate. And even if you somehow manage to reach the nuclear warhead's location, there is nothing there – you have simply wasted your time. 
The reinforcements that "have come" haven't actually come, and if they did arrive (if some squad mates were lost earlier), they would start running through walls and get stuck there. Some achievements won't unlock even if you complete all the required conditions, so you will have to play again and there is no guarantee they will unlock next time.

This is just a small part of the bugs that the game is teeming with.

The developers have added a story mode, although it is hard to call it a story as such. But what can we expect from people unfamiliar with the classics of world literature and history?! They used Mikhail Bulgakov as an ancestor of one of the characters and wrote nonsense about him. In fact, Bulgakov was a Russian and Soviet novelist and playwright, born in the Russian Empire in the 19th century. Besides, Bulgakov is a man, so his surname should have been written in the masculine gender. Furthermore, if you compare the biographies of the same character in Red Solstice and Red Solstice 2: Survivors, it is striking that the developers use the words "ancestor" and "descendant" interchangeably, as if they were synonyms, when in fact they are antonyms.

Oh, right – I almost forgot: there were rumours that the game was designed primarily for multiplayer and that the community there was notoriously toxic, but I didn't run into a single living soul online. It looks like that community had already devoured itself by 2026.

Given all the above, only buy this game if you have strong nerves and are willing to deal mainly with in-game bugs rather than enemies. Otherwise, ignore it.

I found this game by searching for the multi-player co-op tags on steam.  If you're looking for that kind of experience, and like challenging games, then this game is for you.  They are reportedly working on a single player mode, but cooperative-multiplayer is where the heart of this game is.

The game IS challenging.  If you are playing at the correct difficulty for your team, you will lose more often then you will win.  

Even though it's early access, the game is very playable.  They've had some buggy patches but they tend to fix them pretty quick.  The devs are on a fast-release cycle and they listen to the community as to what is and isn't working, what's fun and isn't fun, and they participate in the forums.  

Now that the game is more stable, the dev's have been focusing on adding more content (maps, bosses, missions, skills, etc) which is keeping the game fresh and challenging.

If you can get this game on sale, or money isn't a big deal,  I'd definitely recommend the early access version.  If you are on a tight budget, you may want to wait for release.  I have ~500hours on record so far for a $20 game.  So I'm very happy with the value I'm getting.

I cannot recommend this game to most people. My issue with The Red Solstice is that it feels flawed and incomplete, it is plauged by questionable design decisions and poor balancing combined with a steep learning curve. All that being said the game can be quite fun when playing with a few friends of similar experience level and if you have a group of four or more to play and learn this game with you may find something enjoyable here, but for everyone else I would advise staying away. 

The single player campaign is serviceable but quickly gets rote, and the multiplayer component is dissapointing due to many questionable design choices and poor balancing that is made worse by the experience gap new players will face when joining a lobby with veteran players. You'll find yourself confused and more or less useless for a number of hours before being able to contribute to the team, and once you learn how to properly play the game you'll likely find the experience is not at all what you wanted in the first place. The game works against itself in a number of ways that inhibit strategy and interdependence of the classes. The demolitions class for instance will be made almost entirely useless due to the abundance of lootable explosives IF the team even decides to rely on these devices, but more importantly you can beat the game without ever placing a single explosive or launching a single rocket. Indeed most players merely circle the map with auto-fire on while the faster classes loot ammo. There is never really a need to set up static defense, and on the higher difficulties where it would potentially be viable, the cooldown on such abilities makes it impossible anyway. On top of this few teams will think about their location in relation to enemy units and often times are in the line of fire of heavy ordinance which makes it impossible to use without killing a friendly. The depth of the class system is diminished by the nature of the game.

The other big problem The Red Solstice has is it's pacing. It encourages players to never stop moving. The looting, securing objectives, activating power nodes, etc all happen while on the run. Setting up a static defense is simply not supported, there is no way to lockdown doors, and even items like barricades are useless... not as in poorly implimented, as in the developers never bothered to apply collision detection to them so enemies walk right through these barricades. All slower, and defense oriented classes fail to play as one would expect as a result of this, and indeed the game becomes about patroling the map rather than each class utilizing it's niche focus to support the team. The game really only feels like it has 3 classes, the Medic, and then the rest being a DPS varient, with one acting as a fast looter. This game would be far better if it allowed for setting up actual fortifcations to secure areas and encouraged players to balance offense and defense tactics by establishing a zone of control and having mobile members fetch and secure objectives and luring hordes and large enemies into the heavy fire of your static defense. It would be far better if large enemies required explossive damage to make them vulnerable to small arms fire, it would be far better if it encouraged thinking and planning over running and gunning, especially because the game does not control like a run and gun game. It controls like an RTS, but other than presenting the facade of a strategy game, there is litle strategy to be found. 

I would have liked to have seen the game rely less on bullet sponge enemies and more on forcing players to manage proper firing arcs or face the deadly consequences. Instead the marine behaves in typical rts faction and spins and shoots incoming enemies automatically. The game does provide a manual aim, but it is poorly communicated to the player and the ui for it is terrible. There is no tactical advance in this game, there is no managing firing arcs, there is no establishing a base of operations, there is no flexibility. Like an rts, you group up and blob the enemy and that is a damn shame.

This sort of gameplay was acceptable when it was a modifcation for a 2003 strategy game, it is not acceptable as a stand alone title, and rather than evolve the concept they ripped it almost unchanged from the mod which inspired it. I am hopeful that with the next game in this franchise they are able to get things right, but from the looks of it so far it appears to be a less interesting alien swarm. 

I would advise the developers to look at titles like full spectrum warrior which required establishing firing arcs and moving the squad tactically. Translated to the rts perspective something like that could work well and better define the pace and balance of gameplay.

As a stand alone genre this type of game is still new, and with that comes some hiccups. I applaud these developers for trying to establish this genre, unfortunately the title is too bogged down by the mods that inspired it.

Let me tell you something straightaway: you're going to die, no two ways about it; either it'll be some jackaloon in your squad with an itchy trigger finger and a grenade launcher, or it'll be a bio-engineered thunderbeast from the seventieth dimension of Hentai Mountain using its tentacles on you in ways it's best not to describe in polite company. Your death is more or less inevitable.

The question is: How are you going to face that death?

Crying like a coward and blaming your teammates for leaving you stranded in a distant corner because you wanted that shiny little +5% to weapon damage, the legion of GWAR fans on your tail be damned?

Laughing at the ludicrous nature of the spiky-humpbeast which is making your backside its domain?

Screaming bloody murder as you drop a SHIVA TacNuke device on your now overrun position?

Staring in mute amazement, your head ripped clean off and sailing through the air, as that jackass whose been surviving alone the entire game activates the Evac and then gets there first, spawning wave after wave of the gigantic 'hatchlings' which have just de-crowned you?

Sobbing deeply and sadly as your small, insignificant life snuffed out before it even began, kicked at random by lobby host after lobby host for no reason other than the fact that they like skulls and your name had one next to it? 

You will die, it's as simple and indifferent as that. But how you face that death? That choice is yours.

5/10 "Easy" is just a codeword for 'slightly (1%) less tentacles'
10/10 Getting into an Evac before the entire team and being the only one to survive, Would do again.

The red clouds part, the dropship lands at an unknown location; and 8 marines set down on the Tharsis colony. I've been one of those marines a few hundred times, and none of those drops went as planned.

Your team will spend the next hour gathering items and supplies, weathering a constant flow of monsters as they roam the colony. This process begins slow, building to a crescendo as the game progresses. During the last third of the round, the danger's so intense: it requires the entire team working together to survive. This formula produces a unique and often panicked rush back to the dropship as the team tries to evacuate.

There are two kinds of marines: the ones that make it back to the dropship, and the ones left behind. If you're looking for a game with deep mechanics, replayability, and a challenge, look no further.

Then you get into HUGE enemies (7500 hp!) that basically forces you to utilize each soldier's specialty power, such as gunship strafing, artillery beacon, grenade launcher, HE shells, so you can survive the fight. Gunship strafings can take out a large group of enemies, while artillery beacon can be placed then enemy lead over it so the barrage clean them out. Explosives can be placed, mines can be set, and so on. On the other hand, your soldiers can be seriously hit including poison, broken bones, septic wound, and more. Each soldier can only carry 6 items (some of which can have QTY > 1) so item management can be important as no one can carry everything. In RTS mode, movement controls are limited, but once you enter tactical mode, you can move soldiers about and give more individualized orders. Time also slows down tremendously, giving you time to give precise orders, like go here and kill that (and stay there).  

My main gripe with the game is difficulty in accessing all four members of the team, as usually you can only access the team leader. Only in tactical mode can you access all four members. This makes for a very awkward interface when you're the kind of guy that goes after every locker, where you could find inventory from bandages to explosvies.  These are the "crates" in this universe. TRS falls into the genres of things like top-down, 8-player max co-op/PVE, tactical, military sci-fi, survival game with a hint of RPG.

(i mainly talk about the multiplayer section, although trs does have a single player campaign (~10hrs long) and single-player 'survival' modes.)

in multiplayer though, you control a single 'marine' character in a squad of up to 7 other players--you design your marine. The game offers a range of marine 'suits' to choose from before a match starts. These suits range from tank and taunting roles, demolitions, light scout, sheere DPS oriented and other specialized suits. These suits can further be modified with individual skills, power-ups and unlocks related to experience (there is persistent character progression in trs).

If you're familiar with some of the custom survival maps in warcraft3 or perhaps starcraft arcade; maps like NOTD, or undead assault--TRS shares many of the same game features and design. Game matches can last on average from 30mins to 1hr depending on modes and difficulty chosen, as well as the RNG and which missions you end up being tasked to complete as the match progresses.

I think from a distance you can compare games like helldivers or alienswarm to trs, but TRS can be extremely detail and strategy-oriented. High threats and quick team-death can happen from a bad team navigating decision, a mis-use of a powerful skill or item or just innocent ignorance, "what's hal9k for?." The game is not easy, it has a steep learning curve.

TRS is built on an in-house engine as well(!)--something i barely see anymore with game development--and i think in trs's case, a custom engine really allows for that, large-map, enemy-swarm experience.

It's a great game, one of my personal favorites--i recommend to bring friends who may be interested in the experience.

Don't get discouraged by reviews of people who get frustrated by dying early. This is a game that doesn't hold your hand, has a complex system and has quite a learning curve. it is advised for new squads to do easy difficulty first to familiarize. It shines on multiplayer but you have to do your due diligence (i.e. Go through single player, familiarize with items etc.) This game is not about grinding through the ranks. A team of 8 who knows the game  can create new accounts and beat the game while they're all at rank 1. It's about teamwork, respecting the enemies (why most new players die is they don't respect the swarm), achieving goals as a team, and playing your role (as medic, tank, dps/carry, utility, scout, forward observer etc.).  If you are a fan of the old top down squad games like Night of the Dead, Undead Assault and its ilk, this game is for you. If you want a challenging/complex game that requires teamwork and has hero-based system, you'll like this game.

CONS:
- Single player can only give you 10 to 20 hours of fun. Most of the fun is in multiplayer.
- Only a few maps to go through. I believe the devs can create a random map generator. There is a tactical advantage though of knowing the map.
- high difficulty. This is a team game. If the healer doesn't know what to do, or the tank, then the squad will most likely fall. There is a need for a good leader at higher difficulties.
- medium to steep learning curve, depending on how good you want to be.
- if you die early, you will be automatically revived if you are new to the game. However, after a few ranks, there will no longer be an automatic revive. A medic or a mission can revive you, but you will have to wait.

PROS
- Team game. I've played with Europeans, Chinese, Canadians and Americans. A good world we are in. At higher difficulties, you need to talk, so teamspeak would be necessary. There's a different sense of achievement when you defeat a game as a team.
- Hero-based system. You control one character, customize it and change its load out. There are 8 classes that each have a role to play. Mastery of a class is a journey and there are different ways to build a single class.
- Squadron tactics. You have an enemy sniper shooting at 124m away while a swarm is constantly flowing to your team, what do you do? 3 big fatties chasing you? Fast dogs gnawing at one of your team? Some military squad tactics apply, like leapfrog movements, defensive positions, buddy system etc. The squad leaer has a large impact and responsibility.
- Random missions and enemies. Every game is different depending on the mission, the boss spawn etc.

I'm 3.7 hours into Red Solstice and the more I play, the more I like it. Not exactly an easy learning curve, and I was very close to going for a refund a couple times during the first mission.  Tutorial wasn't bad, but didn't cover many things that would have been pretty helpful as a newbie, things that I had to discover on my own.  Now, having done that I'm greatly enjoying it and would probably rate it an 8 out of 10 at this point. Still, having been a computer gamer for many years, I've learned that one doesn't really know the true 'staying power' of any game until you've played it for a week or two.  

I would encourage anyone who gets frustrated in the early going to keep at it. You absolutely need to use the Tactical Mode a LOT to keep yourself alive.  In Tactical mode you can gain true control over your team, so, for example, you can give direct orders for 3 of your team to cover the one who's deploying satchels or resonators instead of relying on autoaim to protect you.  You can manuever much more effectively, and you also get a more personal feeling about each of your teammates when you're controlling them directly. 

One key thing (at least for me) that I didn't figure out until my third attempt at the first mission is that the GDD device not only points you to nearby monster spawn sites, it also points you to nearby resonators, which you must have to destroy the spawn sites. Without a resonator when you need it, the spawn sites will just continually churn out mobs, and the more functioning spawn sites, the more mobs until eventually you die a horrid, screaming death.

So use the GDD to find the resonators and you'll find survival isn't really impossible.

Good luck, and if this has the kind of staying power I think it will, my only complaint may be that there aren't enough single player missions to keep me happy, so I'll hope for some DLC in the not too distant future.

Con's:

Some small advices:
- Movement speed should be at least 4.5
- Always move unless the mission doesn't let you right now.
- Only shoot at things that are moving fast than you! (The big high HP Enemies are killed with explosives!)
- Use Manual-Aim (shift key) as much as possible - you are doing more dmg this way and can't miss like auto-fire does!
- only move into rooms which leads you into another / outside - don't trap yourself.
- You don't have to loot anymore after level/wave ~9 - you should have everything by now.
- Restart the game after every match.
- If you don't know anything - please ask the ppl ingame to explain stuff.

I have pretty mixed feelings about this game. Sometimes it is genuinely fun, and other times it gets boring fast.

The single-player feels rushed and mostly seems to exist for people who care about the story. It is not terrible, but it is nothing special either. The real focus is clearly on the multiplayer.

That is where the game is at its best. You can play with up to 8 players across 6 different maps, with several difficulty modes to choose from. The problem is that the maps do not really feel all that different. They mostly look the same, with structures just placed in different spots. Matches are built around 15 waves, with different enemy types spawning from multiple locations, so sticking with your team matters. If you wander off on your own, you can get overwhelmed very quickly.

The teamwork aspect is one of the better parts of the game. It creates some tense moments, and the different skills and classes give you some room to play the way you want. With a good team, even the harder parts feel manageable.

The issue is content. Once you have played through the maps and tried most of the modes, the game starts to feel repetitive. Some people will probably love that loop and keep coming back, but for me it did not have enough variety to stay interesting for long.

So yeah, I do not really love this game, but I do not hate it either. It sits right in that awkward middle ground where I can see the fun in it, but I can also feel the boredom creeping in after a while.

Pros
Creates tense moments
Nice variety in skills and classes
Teamwork actually matters

Cons
Can get boring after a while
Needs more varied content

In the end, this is one of those games that is decent with friends, but not something I would keep playing for a long time unless you really enjoy the core loop.

I wanted to put a couple hours into the game before I wrote a good review so here it goes. TRS is a different kind of game, that goes unsaid, if you are not into working with a team via a Chat client (Teamspeak, mumble, etc) you may see some real let downs come gameplay time. Like any other stragety game knowing what the game plan is for your team is important and without a solid communication system you will see teams in public lobbies fall before wave 10. 
Good news is that there is a teamspeak server dedicated to TRS (ts.game-com.de) and as a new player to the game I can say my experience went from crappy, to excellent the moment I signed on there and began playing with people. Not only do you learn a lot from more experienced players (Veterans) but you get to learn a lot of things you wouldn't find out by playing in random lobbies with random people. 

"But Dagnome, there is a in game chat"
True, but like most games with built in VOIP it isn't very good or used at all. 

To sum up, if you are looking for a great team game to play with your friends then TRS will hit that sweet tooth, it can be frustrating because on teammate can screw up the whole game, but it can also be very rewarding like the time me (Medic) and an assault survived together after our team was slaughtered and evaced to safety (http://www.twitch.tv/dagnom/v/7696891).

No game has the right to be this much fun for such a cheap price.
